title: PREX registry HTTP binding
$comment: Wire shapes for a registry that serves package manifests. Endpoint and pagination shapes follow the MCP registry's generic contract deliberately: cursor plus updatedSince is a complete mirror protocol, and there is no reason to invent a second one. What differs is that a PREX registry publishes a Registry Definition, so which of these endpoints exist is discoverable rather than described in prose, and that published documents are signed, so a mirror verifies rather than trusts.

Cursor.$comment: Opaque to clients. A registry may encode a key and a watermark; a client that parses one has coupled itself to an implementation.

count.$comment: Entries in this page, not the total. A total would force a registry to count a federated result set it is streaming.

nextCursor.$comment: Absent or null means this page was the last one. A client MUST NOT treat an empty page as the end while a cursor is still present.

unavailable.$comment: Sources that did not answer. Present so a caller can tell 'nothing matched' from 'a source was down' — a mirror that reads an outage as an empty result concludes it has caught up.

searchMode.$comment: Which search ran. A registry quietly falling back to a full scan is indistinguishable from one that is fast until it is not, and `LIKE '%x%'` cannot use an index — the shape behind the MCP registry's 20-25 second reads.

RegistryEntry.$comment: One package version as a registry serves it: the publisher's manifest, plus what the registry itself asserts about it.

signatures.$comment: Over formatDigest(manifestDigest), as SignedReceipt does it. Present when the registry or the publisher signed; absent is a registry that offers nothing to verify.

RegistryMetadata.$comment: What the registry asserts, kept apart from what the publisher wrote. The MCP registry stamps this into _meta under a reserved key; PREX puts it in a named field because mixing registry assertions into a publisher's document is how provenance stops being attributable.

sourceId.$comment: Which of the registry's configured sources produced this. Present when the registry is relaying rather than serving something published to it — the difference between what it holds and what it fronts.

redirectedFrom.$comment: The name the client actually asked for, when it has moved. Stated rather than silently substituted: a client that gets back a different package than it requested has no way to notice, and a lockfile should record what it resolved.

redirects.$comment: The chain that was followed, so a client can fetch and verify each signed redirect rather than take the registry's word that the move happened.

NamespaceProof.$comment: A signature proves a document was not altered; it says nothing about who may use a name. This binds a signing key to a name prefix. The two are independent and neither substitutes for the other.

namespace.$comment: Reverse-DNS name prefix, e.g. com.example or io.github.someone.

evidence.$comment: What the registry read to satisfy itself: the TXT record, or the URL fetched. Recorded so the decision is auditable after the fact.

RegistryPublishRequest.$comment: Named RegistryPublishRequest, not PublishRequest: the extensions schema already has one for pushing an artifact descriptor to OCI, and the two are different operations. The publisher signs; the registry verifies before it stores. A registry that accepts an unsigned manifest is choosing to be the only thing anyone can check.

Serviceability.$comment: Whether what a manifest advertises still answers. Absent means nobody has looked, which is a different claim from having looked and found it fine.

state.$comment: `gated` is healthy: a service answering 401/402/403 is running and wants credentials the registry does not have. `unchecked` covers timeouts and 5xx, which are evidence about the network between the registry and the origin, not about the package.

method.$comment: What was actually done. Reachable is not the same claim as 'these are the right bytes'.

effective.$comment: A routine rotation must not invalidate everything a key ever signed, and a theft must. `from-now` keeps signatures made before revokedAt valid and stops the key publishing; `retroactive` invalidates every signature it ever made. Collapsing the two forces an operator to choose between an unusable registry and an unrevoked compromise.

replacedBy.$comment: The key that took over, when this was a rotation.

RevocationList.$comment: Signed, because a revocation a client cannot verify is a rumour — and an attacker who can strip or forge one has undone the signing scheme. `serial` and `expiresAt` exist so a client can tell a stale copy from a current one and refuse to be pinned to an old list by a mirror that stopped updating.

serial.$comment: Monotonic. A client that has seen a higher serial must refuse a lower one, or a replay pins it to a list from before a compromise.

KeyRotation.$comment: A new key attested by its predecessor. Continuity is the point: signatures made before the rotation still verify against the old key, while the old key can no longer publish. Without this a publisher rotating a key must re-sign every version they ever published, which is what makes people not rotate.

nextPublicKey.$comment: Ed25519 public JWK for the incoming key.

signature.$comment: By the previous key, over the canonical digest of this document with the signature field absent.

HolderId.$comment: Who holds a namespace, not merely which key signed for it. A survey of the MCP registry found one domain behind 75 namespaces, 62 of them serving a marketing page — visible only to somebody who went and looked. Recording the holder at proof time makes that a query instead of a research project, and it is what a quota can be charged against: 75 namespaces under one domain are one publisher and must share one budget.

namespace.$comment: Reverse-DNS name prefix, e.g. com.example or io.github.someone.

PublishQuota.$comment: Charged per holder, never per namespace. A limit per namespace is not a limit: registering another namespace is exactly the cheap move the holder identity exists to make visible.

PackageRedirect.$comment: A name that moved. A publisher migrating from io.github.someone to com.their-company should not have to ask a maintainer, and the packages that pinned the old name should not stop resolving. Kept as a document rather than an HTTP 308 so a mirror can verify the move actually came from the party that held both names.

reason.$comment: A rename keeps the same holder; a transfer changes it. Both need the outgoing holder's signature, and recording which happened is the difference between 'we moved' and 'we handed it over'.

signatures.$comment: The publisher signature must come from a key holding BOTH names. One name is not enough: a key that holds only the destination could otherwise claim any package it liked, and a key that holds only the source could redirect its users to somebody else's package.
